periods.activity_title: Meet the Animals: Hearing and Joining the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Words — What do You do? (pp.34–35): call-and-response recitation with animal actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud from Textbook pp.34–35, pointing to each animal name. Students listen and observe any pictures, noticing what each animal says it does.

Teacher models the call-and-response: teacher speaks the refrain 'Who are you? And what do you do?' and the class joins in as each animal group, adding a simple action (flap arms for birds, jump for monkeys, etc.).

Fun with Words — What do You do? ("call-and-response recitation with actions"). Class splits into two groups: one asks the refrain, the other responds as each animal in turn, all six stanzas through, with actions.

Quick whole-class chant: all six animals in a single unbroken run, alternating sides at speed. Teacher pauses after any animal to ask 'What did the dogs do?' or 'What do cats do in the dark?' to check understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's repeating refrain 'Who are you? And what do you do?' is its chief scaffold — students who hear it enough times will answer unprompted, so offer several rounds before splitting groups. Watch for children conflating animals (e.g. assigning 'roar' to dogs); gently redirect by pointing to the relevant stanza on the page.

periods.activity_title: Animal Voices: Fluent Recitation and Action Performance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Words — What do You do? (pp.34–35): role-play recitation, each group as one named animal.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a quick choral warm-up of the refrain 'Who are you? And what do you do?' from Textbook pp.34–35, with the whole class responding together for all six animals in sequence.

Fun with Words — What do You do? ("role-play recitation, each group as one named animal"). Six small groups are each assigned one animal; each group rehearses its two-line response with a matching action (e.g. elephants raise arms as trunks, lions cup hands and roar).

Groups perform in textbook order: teacher or a student volunteer calls the refrain, each animal group rises, recites its two lines, performs its action, then sits. Rotate so every child has at least one turn speaking aloud.
Brief share-out: teacher asks two or three children to say one thing an animal in the poem does, using the pattern 'The ___ can ___.' This closes the recitation on the poem's action-word idea.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together in the previous round of recitation, children now inhabit individual animal roles — this shift from unison to group identity deepens both fluency and expression. Encourage expressive volume and movement; the poem's playful tone rewards physical performance rather than quiet reading.

items.item_stem: Listen carefully. Your teacher will say: 'Who are you? And what do you do?' Choose the answer that correctly completes what the monkeys say in the poem.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student has confused birds' response with the monkeys' stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student has attributed the dogs' actions to the monkeys.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has confused the cats' nighttime response with the monkeys'.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will call out: 'Who are you? And what do you do?' Pretend you are the lions from the poem. Stand up, say the lions' two lines aloud, and show a lion action while you speak.

expected_elements: Says 'We are lions' clearly and confidently.
Includes both action words: roar and hunt.
Performs a matching physical action while speaking.
